title: Airworthiness Directives; Polskie Zakłady Lotnicze Sp. z o.o. Airplanes
summary:
The Federal Register just published two safety-focused rules: one from the Federal Aviation Administration requiring immediate checks on a specific part of certain PZL M28 05 airplanes, and another from the Environmental Protection Agency that sets new notice requirements before some chemicals can be used in new ways.

On the aviation side, the FAA is making operators of PZL M28 05 aircraft inspect the area where the rudder control unit mounts to the rear fuselage (known as Frame 29). Cracked or loose bolts were found, which could lead to loss of rudder control. The inspection must be done before the next flight and uses a close visual check with magnification; any problems must be fixed right away, and some follow-up checks may be required. No special flight permits are allowed to move an aircraft before it’s inspected. The rule takes effect November 19, 2025, though an emergency version is already in force, and comments are open through December 19. The FAA estimates nine U.S. aircraft are affected and pegs the basic inspection at about $85 in labor, with repair costs varying by findings.

This move primarily benefits pilots, passengers, and the communities they fly over by reducing the risk of control issues in flight. It also helps operators by catching problems early. On the downside, operators may face unexpected downtime and repair expenses, and aircraft could be grounded until inspections and fixes are complete. That can be especially tough for smaller fleets or time-sensitive missions.

On the chemical policy side, the EPA’s rule requires companies to notify the agency at least 90 days before making, importing, or processing certain listed chemicals for new types of uses. That notice triggers a review to assess potential risks, and the new use can’t begin until the review is finished. The rule takes effect January 5, 2026.

Public health, workers, and the environment stand to benefit from earlier scrutiny of new uses that could create exposure or hazards. Companies that handle these chemicals may face added lead time, planning complexity, and compliance costs. Some projects could be delayed while the agency completes its review, though the process also provides clearer expectations about what is needed to move forward.

Both actions reflect a precautionary approach: act quickly when there’s a credible safety concern, invite public input, and adjust as more information comes in.
